title: SQL Server CPU reaches 95% after a release
description: Diagnose a query-plan regression or parameter-sniffing issue that causes SQL Server CPU to spike after deployment, using Query Store, DMVs, and execution-plan forensics.

data.text: The deployment completed successfully. The tests passed. But within minutes, SQL Server CPU climbs to 95% and stays there. The release changed something in the query plan cache: a new stored procedure, an altered index, or a parameter sniffing event that caused SQL Server to choose a plan optimized for a different data distribution. Query Store is your forensic tool—it captures every plan before and after the release, letting you identify the exact query that regressed and the exact plan change that caused it.

data.title: Core concepts
items: Parameter sniffing: SQL Server compiles a plan using the first execution's parameter values, which may be suboptimal for other values
Plan cache bloat: excessive unique query plans caused by dynamic SQL, implicit conversions, or frequent schema changes
Statistics histogram: stores the distribution of values in a column, used by the optimizer to estimate cardinality
Query Store: a SQL Server feature that captures query plans and performance metrics over time
Forced plan: a known-good execution plan that SQL Server uses for a specific query, bypassing recompilation

terms.definition: SQL Server compiles a query plan using the parameter values from the first execution, which may be suboptimal for subsequent executions with different values.
Excessive unique query plans in the plan cache caused by dynamic SQL, implicit conversions, or frequent schema changes.
A SQL Server object that stores the distribution of values in a column, used by the query optimizer to estimate cardinality.

items: Identify the top CPU-consuming queries using sys.dm_exec_query_stats and sys.dm_exec_sql_text
Check for new or changed queries introduced in the recent release
Review execution plans for scans, key lookups, and expensive sorts or hashes
Update outdated statistics on the affected tables with UPDATE STATISTICS
Kill or pause the deployment if CPU is causing timeouts for critical user paths
Consider enabling Query Store to capture plan regressions automatically

cards.title: Plan Guides or Forced Plans
cards.description: Force SQL Server to use a known-good execution plan for a specific query.
cons: Requires Query Store or plan guides

cards.title: Index Tuning
cards.description: Add covering indexes or adjust existing indexes to eliminate scans and key lookups.
cons: Takes time to design and test

cards.title: Query Rewrite
cards.description: Modify the application query to avoid constructs that trigger bad plans, such as functions on indexed columns.
cons: May not be possible with ORM-generated SQL

data.caption: SQL Server CPU spike investigation flow after a release
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Release Deployed] --> B[CPU Spikes to 95%]
    B --> C[Check Query Store]
    C --> D{New Plan?}
    D -->|Yes| E[Force Previous Plan]
    D -->|No| F[Check Stats Age]
    F --> G{Outdated?}
    G -->|Yes| H[Update Statistics]
    G -->|No| I[Check Missing Index DMVs]
    I --> J[Add Index or Rewrite Query]
    E --> K[Monitor CPU]
    H --> K
    J --> K

items: Query sys.dm_exec_requests to see currently running queries and their CPU time.
Join sys.dm_exec_query_stats with sys.dm_exec_sql_text to find the highest-CPU queries since the last restart.
Compare the execution plans before and after the release using Query Store.
Check for implicit conversions that prevent index seeks.
Review recent schema changes: new columns, altered data types, or added constraints.
Verify that auto-update statistics is enabled and recent enough for the workload.

data.title: Do not shrink the plan cache
data.text: Clearing the plan cache (DBCC FREEPROCCACHE) releases pressure temporarily but causes every query to recompile, often making CPU worse. Use it only as a last-resort emergency measure.

items: Enable Query Store on all production databases to track plan regressions
Set up automatic alerts for CPU usage exceeding 80% for more than 5 minutes
Run database performance tests in CI for queries that change in each release
Review execution plans for new or modified queries before merging
Schedule regular index and statistic maintenance during low-traffic windows
Use forced plans or plan guides only as a temporary bridge while fixing queries

items.question: Why did the CPU spike only after the release, not during testing?
items.answer: Test environments often have smaller data sets and lower concurrency. Parameter sniffing and plan regressions may only manifest with production data volume and parameter distributions.

items.question: Is high CPU always caused by queries?
items.answer: Not always. High CPU can also come from compilation storms, plan cache bloat, or background tasks like index maintenance. Check sys.dm_os_ring_buffers for SOS_SCHEDULER_YIELD waits.

data.title: Diagnose a post-release CPU spike
data.description: A SQL Server database jumps to 95% CPU after a deployment. The release included three changed stored procedures. Use Query Store and DMVs to identify the culprit and propose a fix.
steps: Retrieve the top five CPU-consuming queries since the release
Compare their execution plans with plans from before the release
Identify the specific query with the largest plan regression
Propose a fix: index, rewrite, or forced plan
Validate the fix by running the query with representative parameter values
data.expectedOutcome: You should identify a regressed query plan, explain why it regressed, and implement a fix that reduces CPU back to baseline.

data.title: Summary
points: CPU spikes after releases are often query plan regressions
Use Query Store to compare plans before and after the release
Fix root causes with indexes or query rewrites, not plan cache clearing
Test queries with production data volumes before merging
Monitor CPU continuously and alert early
data.takeaway: SQL Server CPU spikes are usually predictable from query plan changes. Treat Query Store as your primary forensic tool and never skip execution plan review in code changes that touch data access.
